column1: 1:1|The word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai:|Keeps the standard commissioning opening and full parentage.

1:2|“Get up and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim against it, because their evil has come up before me.”|Preserves great city and evil rising into divine presence rather than supplying the proclamation's later content.

1:3|Jonah got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the LORD’s presence. He went down to Joppa, found a ship bound for Tarshish, paid its fare, and went down aboard to travel with them to Tarshish, away from the LORD’s presence.|Keeps all three Tarshish mentions, both presence clauses, and repeated downward motion central to the narrative.

1:4|But the LORD hurled a great wind onto the sea. A great storm rose on the sea, and the ship was on the point of breaking apart.|Uses hurled to connect divine wind with sailors' later hurling; retains doubled great.

1:5|The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his god. They hurled the cargo into the sea to lighten the ship. Meanwhile Jonah had gone down into the hold, lain down, and fallen fast asleep.|Preserves each sailor's god, cargo disposal, Jonah's further descent, and sleep contrast.

1:6|The captain came to him and said, “What are you doing asleep? Get up and call on your god! Perhaps the god will take notice of us, and we will not perish.”|Repeats get up/call from the commission and preserves the captain's perhaps.

1:7|The sailors said to one another, “Come, let us cast lots to find out who has brought this disaster on us.” They cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.|Keeps repeated casting and result without endorsing the procedure as generally reliable.

1:8|They asked him, “Tell us, please, who is responsible for this disaster? What is your work? Where do you come from? What is your country? What people do you belong to?”|Preserves all five urgent questions rather than condensing the interrogation.

1:9|He answered, “I am a Hebrew. I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”|Retains fear as recurring motif and the irony of confessing the maker of the sea while fleeing across it.

1:10|The men became terribly afraid and asked, “What have you done?” They knew he was fleeing from the LORD’s presence, because he had told them.|Keeps intensified fear and the narrator's explanation of their knowledge.
1:11|They asked, “What should we do with you so the sea will calm down for us?” The sea was growing more and more stormy.|Retains the practical question and progressive storm intensity.

1:12|He told them, “Pick me up and hurl me into the sea. Then the sea will calm down for you. I know this great storm has come upon you because of me.”|Preserves Jonah's own proposed remedy and responsibility claim without inventing his motive.

1:13|Instead, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not. The sea kept growing stormier against them.|Makes their attempted alternative clear and repeats worsening sea and dry land.

1:14|Then they called to the LORD: “Please, LORD, do not let us perish for this man’s life, and do not charge us with innocent blood. For you, LORD, have done as you pleased.”|Retains all three divine names and the sailors' explicit fear of bloodguilt.
1:15|They picked Jonah up and hurled him into the sea, and the sea stopped raging.|Repeats the commanded action and immediate cessation without extra miraculous commentary.
1:16|Then the men feared the LORD greatly. They offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.|Preserves fear's new object and both worship acts without relocating them to shore.

1:17|The LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was inside the fish for three days and three nights.|Keeps fish unspecified, appointed as recurring verb, and exact duration; maps Hebrew2:1 to public1:17.
2:1|From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God.|Preserves setting and personal divine relationship without claiming a different fish from grammatical gender.

2:2|He said:
“In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me.
From the belly of Sheol I cried for help,
and you heard my voice.|Keeps past-tense thanksgiving and shift from he to you, with Sheol distinct from fish belly.
2:3|You cast me into the depths, into the heart of the seas.\nThe current surrounded me;\nall your breakers and waves swept over me.|Preserves Jonah's attribution to God and possessive your waves.
2:4|I said, ‘I have been driven out of your sight,\nyet I will look again toward your holy temple.’|Chooses yet-affirmation while noting possible question; retains temple orientation.
2:5|Water closed over me to the throat;\nthe deep surrounded me.\nSeaweed was wrapped around my head.|Uses throat for nephesh in drowning context and keeps tangible weed detail.

2:6|I went down to the roots of the mountains;
the earth’s bars closed behind me forever.
But you brought my life up from the pit,
LORD my God.|Preserves downward/upward reversal and ancient underworld gates without modernizing cosmology.
2:7|As my life was ebbing away, I remembered the LORD.\nMy prayer came to you, into your holy temple.|Keeps remembered divine name then direct address and repeated temple.
2:8|Those who cling to worthless vanities\nabandon their faithful love.|Retains ambiguous their hesed rather than deciding only grace offered them or loyalty owed.

2:9|But I will sacrifice to you with a voice of thanksgiving.\nWhat I have vowed, I will fulfill.\nDeliverance belongs to the LORD!”|Keeps vow/sacrifice parallels to sailors and climactic divine ownership of rescue.
2:10|The LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.|Preserves the deliberately physical verb and dry-land motif without euphemism.
3:1|The word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time:|Repeats the commission opening with explicit second chance.
3:2|“Get up and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim to it the message I give you.”|Preserves the changed to-it wording and message dependence.

3:3|Jonah got up and went to Nineveh as the LORD had said. Nineveh was a city great before God, a three-day journey.|Retains lelohim instead of erasing God as mere intensifier and leaves journey's measurement unresolved.

3:4|Jonah began to enter the city, going a day’s journey. He proclaimed, “Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overturned!”|Keeps forty, one-day progress, and overturned with its destruction/transformation range.

3:5|The people of Nineveh believed God. They proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least.|Preserves belief's object and social extent without inventing details of conversion.

3:6|When the news reached Nineveh’s king, he rose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.|Keeps king of Nineveh as given and four successive abasement actions.

3:7|He had this proclamation issued in Nineveh: “By decree of the king and his nobles: No person or animal, herd or flock, may taste anything. They must not graze or drink water.|Retains nobles' participation and the unusual inclusion of animals in the fast.

3:8|Let people and animals be covered with sackcloth. Let them call urgently to God. Let everyone turn from their evil way and from the violence in their hands.|Keeps animals clothed and concrete violence as target of change rather than only ritual action.
3:9|Who knows? God may turn and relent, turning from his burning anger so that we do not perish.”|Retains the uncertainty and repeated turning rather than claiming a guaranteed bargain.

3:10|God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way. God relented from the disaster he had said he would bring on them, and he did not bring it.|Preserves the deeds/turning basis, repeated God, and evil/disaster wordplay in contextual senses.
4:1|But to Jonah this seemed a great wrong, and he burned with anger.|Retains raah link to evil/disaster as Jonah's evaluation and heat of anger, not narrator endorsement.

4:2|He prayed to the LORD: “Please, LORD, isn’t this what I said while I was still in my own country? That is why I fled toward Tarshish in the first place. I knew you were a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and rich in faithful love, who relents from bringing disaster.|Keeps both names, revealed flight motive, and the complete shared mercy formula as Jonah's complaint.
4:3|Now, LORD, please take my life from me. I would be better off dead than alive.”|Preserves explicit request for death as character speech without softening it into discouragement.
4:4|The LORD asked, “Is it right for you to be angry?”|Retains the evaluative question with intensity alternative noted.

4:5|Jonah went out of the city and sat to its east. He made himself a shelter there and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city.|Keeps east, shelter, shade, and waiting without rearranging chronology.

4:6|The LORD God appointed a plant, which grew up over Jonah to shade his head and relieve his distress. Jonah was greatly delighted with the plant.|Preserves combined divine title, appointed motif, and great delight contrasting great wrong; species left unspecified.
4:7|At dawn the next day, God appointed a worm. It attacked the plant, and the plant withered.|Keeps timing, repeated appointed, and causal plant death.

4:8|When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind. The sun beat down on Jonah’s head until he grew faint. He asked to die, saying, “I would be better off dead than alive.”|Preserves appointed third agent and repeated death speech; rare wind adjective noted.

4:9|God asked Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the plant?” He answered, “It is right for me to be angry—angry enough to die!”|Repeats the evaluative question and Jonah's intensified self-justification.

4:10|The LORD said, “You have compassion for the plant, though you did not labor over it or make it grow. It came into being in a night and perished in a night.|Keeps compassion and repeated overnight brevity as the comparison's grounds.

4:11|Should I not have compassion for Nineveh, the great city, with more than 120,000 people who cannot distinguish their right hand from their left—and many animals?”|Preserves the open final question, more-than count, unresolved right/left idiom, and final animals.
